| Observed behavior | Likely cause | Next step | Pro needed? |
Fill rows that match the reported and testable behaviors.

Verdict: ...
Confidence: Low/Medium/High
Next Action: ...

examples.title: Breaker trips instantly on reset
examples.input: 15 amp breaker for my bathroom. I reset it and it trips again right away even though nothing is plugged in. No smell or heat.
examples.output:
## ⚠️ SAFETY GATE
No immediate hazard flags reported — proceed with caution.

## RANKED LIKELY CAUSES
1. Short Circuit — immediate re-trip with no load strongly suggests hot-to-neutral/ground contact in the wiring or a fixture.
2. Ground Fault — bathroom circuits are often GFCI-protected; a damaged device or moisture can cause instant trips.
3. Faulty Breaker — worn breakers can trip on reset, but this is less likely than a wiring fault.

## ISOLATION PROCEDURE
1. Confirm every light switch on the circuit is OFF and nothing is plugged into bathroom outlets.
2. Flip the breaker fully to OFF, then firmly back to ON.
3. If it still trips with zero load, do NOT keep resetting it — the fault is in fixed wiring or a fixture.
4. If a GFCI outlet is on this circuit, press its RESET button and retest.

## SYMPTOM → CAUSE → ACTION TABLE
| Observed behavior | Likely cause | Next step | Pro needed? |
| Trips instantly with no load | Short circuit in wiring/fixture | Stop resetting; electrician to locate fault | Yes |
| Trips only when GFCI involved | Ground fault | Press GFCI reset once; if it re-trips, call pro | Yes |

## 🛑 STOP AND CALL A PRO IF
- Breaker re-trips instantly with nothing connected (your case).
- You would need to open the panel or swap the breaker.
- Any heat, smell, or spark appears.

## 📋 COPY-PASTE SUMMARY
Verdict: Likely short circuit or ground fault in fixed wiring; not a DIY fix.
Confidence: Medium
Next Action: Leave breaker OFF and contact a licensed electrician.
Pro Needed: Yes
Note: Local electrical codes and permit requirements may apply; when in doubt, hire a licensed electrician.

examples.title: Breaker trips only under load
examples.input: 20A kitchen breaker. Holds fine until I run the microwave and toaster at the same time, then it trips. No smell.
examples.output:
## ⚠️ SAFETY GATE
No immediate hazard flags reported — proceed with caution.

## RANKED LIKELY CAUSES
1. Overload — tripping only when two high-wattage appliances run together is the textbook sign of exceeding the 20A circuit capacity.
2. Loose Connection — a marginal connection can heat under load and trip; less likely but worth noting.
3. Faulty Breaker — a weakened breaker may trip below rated load; least likely here.

## ISOLATION PROCEDURE
1. Reset the breaker (full OFF then firmly ON).
2. Run the microwave alone — note if it holds.
3. Run the toaster alone — note if it holds.
4. Run both together — if it trips only then, the circuit is overloaded.

## SYMPTOM → CAUSE → ACTION TABLE
| Observed behavior | Likely cause | Next step | Pro needed? |
| Trips only with both appliances | Overload | Spread loads across different circuits/outlets | No |
| Trips with one appliance alone | Faulty appliance or breaker | Test appliance on another circuit | Maybe |
| Outlet/plug feels warm | Loose connection | Stop use; call electrician | Yes |

## 🛑 STOP AND CALL A PRO IF
- A single appliance trips the breaker on its own after testing.
- Any outlet, plug, or cord feels warm or smells.
- Tripping continues even after separating the loads.

## 📋 COPY-PASTE SUMMARY
Verdict: Circuit overload from running two high-wattage appliances on one 20A circuit.
Confidence: High
Next Action: Run the microwave and toaster on separate circuits; avoid simultaneous use.
Pro Needed: No
Note: Local electrical codes and permit requirements may apply; when in doubt, hire a licensed electrician.

## Instructions

3. Classify the most probable cause into one of: Overload, Short Circuit, Ground Fault, Faulty/Worn Breaker, or Loose Connection — ranked by likelihood with a one-line rationale each.
4. Provide a numbered ISOLATION PROCEDURE: unplug/turn off everything on the circuit, fully flip breaker OFF then firmly ON, reconnect loads one at a time, and note which load reprovokes the trip.

6. Always include an explicit STOP-AND-CALL-A-PRO list and never advise opening the service panel, replacing a breaker, or touching wiring unless the user already stated competence; default to non-invasive steps.
7. End with a copy-pasteable summary block (Verdict, Confidence, Next Action, Pro Needed Y/N) suitable for pasting into notes or sending to an electrician.
8. Include jurisdiction-neutral caveats and remind the user that local electrical codes and permit rules may apply.
